analysis.one_liner: Phases out federal price supports and quotas for the sugar industry over four years.
analysis.headline: Despite 73 cosponsors from both parties, the bill never got a committee vote, and the sugar price-support program it would have phased out stayed in place.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would cut the federal loan rate for sugarcane processors from 18 cents to 14 cents per pound between 1999 and 2002, convert the government's no-lose loans into regular loans that borrowers must repay, end all federal price support for sugar after the 2002 crop, and repeal the Depression-era quota system that hands growers guaranteed shares of the sugar market. It would also require the President to make sure sugar reaches the U.S. market at prices no higher than the higher of the world price or the loan rate.
analysis.who_benefits: American consumers, who pay for the sugar program through higher grocery prices, and food and beverage makers that buy sugar as an ingredient. Taxpayers also benefit because under the current no-lose loan design, the government (and so the public) absorbs losses when sugar prices fall.

how_it_helps.text: Cuts the guaranteed loan rate for raw cane sugar from 18 cents per pound to 17, 16, 15, and then 14 cents across the 1999 through 2002 crops, lowering the price floor that keeps U.S. sugar prices up.

Converts sugar loans from nonrecourse to recourse: under a nonrecourse loan a borrower who cannot sell sugar profitably keeps the government money and hands over the crop, while a recourse loan makes the borrower repay the difference, ending a public backstop for private price risk.

Ends all federal price support — loans, payments, purchases, or other operations — for sugarcane and sugar beet crops from 2003 onward, and repeals the sugar marketing quota and allotment provisions of the 1938 Agricultural Adjustment Act.

Directs the President to use all available authority to ensure raw cane sugar is available to the U.S. market at prices no greater than the higher of the world sugar price or the loan rate, aimed at keeping consumer prices down while the program winds down.

analysis.who_pays: Sugarcane and sugar beet growers and the processors who mill and refine their crops, who would face falling guaranteed prices, full exposure to market risk on loans, loss of federally guaranteed market shares, and complete loss of federal support from the 2003 crop onward. Much of that cost would land in sugar-producing regions like Florida, Louisiana, and the Red River Valley.
analysis.who_pays_short: Sugar growers, processors, and quota holders

drawbacks.text: Eliminating support entirely from the 2003 crop onward would leave sugar growers with no federal safety net at all, a sharper landing than most farm commodities got, and could destabilize farm communities in cane- and beet-growing regions.

Tying the U.S. market to the world sugar price exposes domestic growers to a benchmark that sugar-producing countries support with their own subsidies, a fairness objection growers would raise while the bill phases their program out.
Repealing marketing quotas eliminates guaranteed allotments that carry real market value for growers and landowners, a one-time wealth loss concentrated on those who hold them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The savings flow broadly to every household and food manufacturer in the country through lower sugar prices, while the costs fall on a small, well-organized group of growers and processors. The phase-out design softens the blow with four years of declining support, but the total elimination after 2002 is a genuinely hard cut for sugar regions. On balance the bill shifts money from a concentrated, protected interest to the general public, which is exactly why it faced resistance in committee.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Agriculture Committee and then to its subcommittee on risk management and specialty crops, where it sat for the rest of the two-year Congress without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Dan Miller of Florida introduced the Sugar Program Reform Act on May 18, 1999, with 44 members joining as original cosponsors, including Democrats such as George Miller of California, Waxman, and Stark alongside Republicans such as Goss, Shays, and Sensenbrenner.
The bill attracted 73 total cosponsors, 27 Democrats and 46 Republicans, unusual bipartisan breadth for a subsidy-repeal bill.
The House referred it to the Committee on Agriculture on the day of introduction, and a week later, on May 25, 1999, sent it to the Subcommittee on Risk Management, Research and Specialty Crops.
No further action of any kind is recorded: the subcommittee never reported the bill, and it died there when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sugar growers, processors, and quota holders kept the price supports, no-lose loans, and guaranteed market allotments the bill would have removed, and consumers kept paying program-supported sugar prices. The Agriculture Committee, whose members answer to farm constituencies, avoided a politically difficult vote on a bill with bipartisan support.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Sugar growers and processors kept their supports

for.name: Rep. Dan Miller
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Sugar Program Reform Act and recruited cosponsors across both parties.

for.name: 27 of 211 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including prominent liberals such as George Miller, Waxman, and Stark, giving the repeal effort cross-party cover.

against.name: House Committee on Agriculture (Chair Larry Combest)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to a subcommittee on May 25, 1999 and never brought it to a markup or vote; it died there when the Congress ended.

against.name: Sugar growers and processors
against.what_they_did: Opposed sugar program reform, which would have ended the price supports and quotas underpinning their revenue.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship split 46 Republicans and 27 Democrats, roughly proportional to both parties' House caucuses, so the bill had genuine two-party support; the obstruction came from the committee process, not from a party bloc voting no.

industries.note: Growers depend on federally guaranteed loan rates and marketing quotas that keep U.S. sugar prices above world levels, so their revenue comes directly from what consumers pay at the store. The bill would have phased all of that out.

Processors receive the government loans at guaranteed rates, and converting them to recourse loans would put default risk on the processors themselves instead of the public. The bill cuts their loan rates annually and cuts them off entirely after the 2002 crop.
Candy, baked goods, and beverage makers buy sugar as a major input, and lower U.S. sugar prices flow straight into their costs, sharing the savings with consumers.
